3.2. Soundscape
Ten studies among the 80 included ones were classified as sound-
scape studies regarding perceived or experienced acoustic environment.
In addition to the reduction of the physical noise level, the concept of
improving perceived acoustic environment was applied. The soundscape
was not used as a core search term in the identification process, because
the objective of this study was not reviewing soundscape research but
looking for impacts of building envelope on urban acoustic environ-
ment. As an output of systematic reviewing process, soundscape
approach in order to improve perceived acoustic environment using
building envelopes and street design has been derived. The design of the building façades [96], courtyards [45,100], and
streets [90] might affect noise annoyance. Multisensory integration
approaches have also been studied to enhance outdoor sound percep-
tion. Positive auditory stimuli, visual factors, thermal comfort, and even
olfactory factors affected soundscape quality such as acoustic comfort
and noise annoyance, etc. Natural sounds [50] have been used to
enhance traffic noise perception. Views [82,92,94] have been investi-
gated for road traffic noise annoyance. Recently, the lilac fragrance [97]
was introduced in road traffic noise perception studies. Temperature
[102] has been considered as one of factors affecting soundscape.

excluded for quantitative synthesis. We analysed the remaining 70 ar-
ticles and the 62 articles having insertion loss level due to building en-

noise levels between untreated and treated building envelopes have
been defined and studied in various ways, such as noise reduction, level
differences, noise attenuation, and insertion loss. The term insertion
loss, the most frequently shown in the included articles, was used uni-
formly throughout the study. The dB and dBA scale insertion loss were
